summary: Explains buoyant force (upthrust) as the pressure difference between the top and bottom of a submerged object, derives Archimedes' Principle F_B = rho_f*V_sub*g, covers the Principle of Flotation (sink/float/suspend conditions), and applies these ideas to ships, submarines, and hot-air balloons.
title: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy

summary: Distinguishes streamline (laminar) flow, smooth and predictable, from turbulent flow, chaotic with eddies, defines the theoretical ideal fluid (non-viscous, incompressible, steady, irrotational), and explains why real fluids are viscous due to internal friction between layers.
title: Types of Fluid Flow

summary: Derives the Equation of Continuity from conservation of mass: rho_1*A_1*v_1 = rho_2*A_2*v_2 for real fluids, simplifying to A_1*v_1 = A_2*v_2 for an ideal incompressible fluid, showing fluid speeds up where a pipe narrows and slows where it widens.
title: 6.3 Equation of Continuity

summary: States Bernoulli's Equation P + (1/2)*rho*v^2 + rho*g*h = constant as conservation of energy for an ideal fluid, derives it from the work-energy theorem applied to pressure forces on a moving fluid segment, and notes its limitation to ideal (non-viscous, incompressible) fluids in steady streamline flow.
title: Bernoulli's Equation

summary: Surveys seven practical applications of Bernoulli's Equation: speed of efflux (Torricelli's Theorem), the Venturi effect and meter, filter pumps, atomizers, lift on an aerofoil, the swing of a spinning ball, and blood flow through constricted arteries.
title: Applications of Bernoulli's Equation

summary: States Torricelli's Theorem, v = sqrt(2gh), the speed of efflux from a hole at depth h equals the speed of free fall from that height, and derives it from Bernoulli's Equation using the assumptions of equal atmospheric pressure at both points and a negligible fall speed at the reservoir's top surface.
title: 6.4.2 Torricelli's Theorem

summary: Explains how a Venturi meter measures flow rate by narrowing a pipe (converging section, throat, diverging section) to trade velocity for pressure, and derives the inlet velocity formula V_1 = A_2*sqrt(2gh)/sqrt(A_1^2-A_2^2) by combining Bernoulli's equation with the equation of continuity.
title: Venturi Meter

summary: Explains how an aerofoil generates lift via Bernoulli's principle (F_L = (P_1-P_2)*A) and Newton's third law, covers angle of attack and stalling, and extends the same pressure-difference idea to the Magnus effect that curves a spinning cricket ball.
title: Aerofoil

summary: Defines viscosity (coefficient eta, Pa.s, dimensions ML^-1T^-1) and drag force, states Stokes' Law F_d = 6*pi*eta*r*v for small spheres at low speed, and derives terminal velocity v_t = 2r^2(rho_s-rho_f)g / (9*eta), showing it scales with r^2.
title: Viscosity and Drag

summary: Covers fluid friction (drag) broadly: viscosity's role in generating drag, the general high-velocity drag equation F_D = (1/2)*rho*v^2*C_D*A versus Stokes' Law F=6*pi*eta*r*v for small spheres at low speed, terminal velocity as the force-balance condition, and a real-world streamlining example.
title: Fluid Friction and Drag

summary: Defines terminal velocity as the point where gravitational force balances drag force (net force and acceleration both zero), derives v_t = 2*rho*g*r^2/(9*eta) for a falling sphere using Stokes' Law, and applies the idea to a paratrooper's two-phase jump and everyday conceptual questions about falling objects.
title: Terminal Velocity

summary: Explains superfluidity as zero-viscosity flow (seen below the Lambda Point in Helium-4 and Helium-3), its defining characteristics (persistent motion, high thermal conductivity, quantum coherence), quantized vortex formation under rotation, and real-world applications from gyroscopes to MRI coolants.
title: Superfluidity
